text:
Help me write an open letter. I own an independent pharmacy, and I'm writing for 38 independent pharmacies in our state to the state employees' health plan. We'll send it to the plan and to the two newspapers in the capital.

Facts:
- Since January the plan pays us on average $1.80 less per prescription than it costs us to buy and fill it, for the 20 generic drugs we fill most.
- Plan members make up about 22% of the prescriptions at our 38 pharmacies.
- 9 independent pharmacies in the state closed in the last 2 years. We don't know how many closed because of rates.
- In 14 counties, the nearest pharmacy for most people is an independent one.
- The plan's contract with its pharmacy benefit manager comes up for renewal on July 1.
- My own pharmacy filled about 3,100 prescriptions for plan members last year.

I want the letter to say that a third of the independent pharmacies in the state will close within a year if nothing changes. One page.

Before I draft, I have a few questions. Your answers will change what the letter can say, and how well it holds up when the plan and the reporters read it.

1. **What is the "a third will close within a year" figure based on?** How many independent pharmacies are in the state in total? Did any of the 38 say they'll close or cut back if rates stay the same? The facts you gave me don't support the claim yet. Reporters will ask where it came from, and if it falls apart, the rest of the letter goes with it. If you have a survey, even an informal one, I can use it (for example, "11 of the 38 of us say we cannot stay open past next summer at these rates"). If you don't, I'll write the warning in a way your numbers can back up.

2. **What exactly do you want the plan to do before July 1?** For example: write into the new PBM contract that pharmacies are paid at least what the drug costs plus a set dispensing fee, publish what the PBM pays pharmacies, or meet with you before they sign. Do you have a number or a name for it? Also, who should the letter be addressed to (name and title)?

3. **How does the $1.80 work out?** Is it the drug's purchase price alone, or does it include your cost to fill? Is it only for those 20 generics, and what share of plan prescriptions are those 20? For your own pharmacy: about 3,100 plan prescriptions times $1.80 is roughly $5,600 a year, if all of them were in the losing group. Is that close to right?

4. **The plan will probably say "members can use chain stores or mail order."** Which of the 14 counties could you name? Do you know how far the next pharmacy is in any of them? Have you raised the rates with the plan or the PBM before, and what did they say?

5. **Who signs?** All 38 owners by name and town, or you on behalf of a group? Is there a contact person for reporters?

6. **What will the plan or the papers find out anyway?** For example: some of the 9 closures had other causes, rates on other drugs or other plans make up some of the loss, or your group lobbies on this issue. Anything like that is better addressed in the letter than discovered by a reporter.

If you don't know some of these, just say so. I'll write around the gaps without guessing.

1. I don't have a survey and I don't know the state total. Two of the 38 told me they'll stop filling for plan members if nothing changes. I can't name anyone who will close. Fair point that "a third within a year" goes past what we have, so use a claim the facts support.

2. The July 1 renewal should pay at least what the drug costs us, plus a fill fee. No set number for the fee. I don't have a name or title for who to address it to. We'll share our purchase invoices for the 20 drugs with the plan, and I can meet with the plan's staff any time before May 1.

3. I don't know if it includes the cost to fill, or what share of plan prescriptions those 20 are. So I can't say if the $5,600 is right.

4. In those 14 counties the nearest chain pharmacy is more than 20 miles away for most people. I don't know which counties offhand. I don't know if we've raised it with the plan before.

5. Me on behalf of the group. Tom Reilly, owner of Reilly Drug in Carver, for the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance. I'm the contact.

6. Some of us make up part of the loss on brand-name drugs. I don't know how much. Also, we don't know how many of the 9 closed because of rates.

I wrote the letter around the claim your facts can carry. Pharmacies are already losing money on plan prescriptions. Two of the 38 say they'll stop filling them. In 14 counties, losing the local independent means a 20-mile trip.

<final_document>
**An open letter to the State Employees' Health Plan**
**From 38 independent pharmacies, about the July 1 pharmacy contract**

Since January, the State Employees' Health Plan has paid our pharmacies less than it costs us to fill your members' prescriptions. For the 20 generic drugs we fill most often, the plan pays us on average $1.80 less per prescription than our cost.

That is not a small corner of our business. Plan members account for about 22% of the prescriptions filled at our 38 pharmacies, so more than one prescription in five is a state employee or a family member. Some of us make up part of the loss on brand-name drugs. That covers only part of it, and it doesn't explain why a state plan should pay below cost for the generics we fill most.

This matters most to your members outside the cities. In 14 counties, the nearest pharmacy for most people is an independent one. For most people there, the nearest chain pharmacy is more than 20 miles away. Nine independent pharmacies in this state have closed in the past two years. We don't know how many of them closed because of rates. We do know that two of the 38 pharmacies signing this letter say they'll stop filling prescriptions for plan members if nothing changes. When a pharmacy in one of those counties stops, a state employee who needs a refill has a 40-mile round trip or a mail-order wait.

The plan can fix this, and the date to do it is coming up. Your contract with your pharmacy benefit manager renews on July 1. We ask that the renewed contract require pharmacies to be paid at least what the drug costs them, plus a fee for filling the prescription.

You don't have to take our word for the numbers. We will give your staff our purchase invoices for all 20 drugs so you can check our costs against what the plan pays. I'll meet with your staff any time before May 1, early enough for whatever you learn to go into the contract.

We want to keep filling prescriptions for state employees. We've done it for years, in towns where we are often the only pharmacy. We are asking the plan to make sure that in the July 1 contract, filling a prescription doesn't cost us more than we're paid for it.

Tom Reilly
Owner, Reilly Drug, Carver
On behalf of the Main Street Pharmacy Alliance, 38 independent pharmacies
Contact: [phone] · [email]
</final_document>

Before you send it:

- **The $1.80.** The letter says "less than our cost" because you don't know whether that figure includes the cost of filling. Please check this before May 1, since the plan will see the invoices. If the $1.80 compares the plan's payment to the drug price alone, your real loss per prescription is larger, and you can say so.
- **Fill in the brackets.** Add your phone and email. If you can find out who heads the plan, add a "To:" line with their name.
- **Two things would strengthen it, if you can get them:** the names of a few of the 14 counties, and whether anyone in the group has raised these rates with the plan before. If someone has, the plan will remember it, so one sentence about it ("we raised this with the plan in March") is worth adding.
- I didn't use the $5,600 figure for your pharmacy, and I didn't say how many pharmacies will close. Your facts don't support either one yet.
